glossaryTerms.definition: A liver enzyme responsible for breaking down a large proportion of commonly prescribed drugs. Some herbs (notably St John's wort) activate this enzyme, causing the body to break down drugs faster than intended and lowering their blood level to the point where they stop working.

content.text: Herb and drug interactions: what they are, why they happen, which herbs are most likely to cause them, and how to check before you start a herbal preparation if you are on any prescription medication. This is the most important safety article in the herbal section. Reading it before you start any herbal course if you take prescription drugs is worthwhile.

This article does not replace professional advice. It explains the principles clearly so you can have an informed conversation with a pharmacist, a herbalist, or your prescriber. The conclusion of any such conversation might be that your specific herb and drug combination carries no meaningful risk. That conclusion needs the professional, not the article.
Why interactions happen

Herbs are chemically active. That is the point of them. The same activity that produces a therapeutic effect can also affect how the body handles a prescription drug. Interactions happen in a few ways:
The herb speeds up or slows down the liver enzymes that break down the drug, changing how much of it stays in the blood.
St John's wort induces liver enzymes. It lowers the blood level of many medicines, sometimes to the point of treatment failure.
The herb interferes with how the drug is absorbed from the gut (coating and soothing herbs are the main offenders here).

"Natural" does not mean "no interaction". Most of the significant herb-drug interactions that have been documented involve herbs with centuries of traditional use. The interaction is not evidence the herb is dangerous. It is evidence the herb is chemically active enough to matter.
St John's wort: the most important interaction in herbal medicine
St John's wort is a strong activator of
CYP3A4

, the liver enzyme that breaks down a large number of commonly prescribed drugs. When St John's wort activates this enzyme, drugs are cleared from the bloodstream faster than the prescriber intended. The drug's effect is reduced. In some cases, the drug stops working altogether.

The drugs affected include SSRIs and SNRIs (risk of serotonin syndrome). The contraceptive pill and other hormonal options (reduced effectiveness). Warfarin (reduced anticoagulant effect, risk of clotting). Cyclosporin (transplant rejection risk). HIV antiretrovirals, some anticancer drugs, and other CYP3A4 substrates. The full list is long. If you take any prescription medication, treat St John's wort as incompatible until you have spoken to your prescriber.

The rule for St John's wort is simple: if you are on any prescription medication, speak to your prescriber before using it. This applies to the infusion, the alcohol extract, and the infused oil. The external oil has lower systemic absorption, but the principle holds.
Herbs that affect bleeding and anticoagulants
Several kitchen herbs slow blood clotting. At cooking amounts this rarely matters. At therapeutic doses it can matter if you also take anticoagulant medication.

Ginger has mild antiplatelet activity. Garlic has known antiplatelet activity. Stop it at least a week before surgery. Turmeric at high doses adds to anticoagulant effects. If you are on warfarin, aspirin therapy, clopidogrel, or any other anticoagulant. Keep these herbs to culinary levels while on medication and discuss therapeutic doses with your prescriber.
Sedative herbs and sedative drugs

Valerian, hops, and passionflower all have mild sedating effects. They add to the effect of sleeping tablets, anxiety medication, and other sedating drugs. Do not combine them with prescription sedatives without telling your prescriber. The same caution applies to driving.
Liquorice and cardiac medication

Liquorice root at therapeutic doses slows cortisol breakdown. This raises blood pressure and lowers potassium levels. It greatly interacts with digoxin and antihypertensives. Anyone on cardiac medication should avoid therapeutic liquorice doses.
Marshmallow, slippery elm, and drug absorption

Marshmallow root and slippery elm bark are both coating and soothing herbs: they produce a thick, gel-like coating when prepared in water. This is the action that makes them useful for a sore throat or an irritated gut lining. The same coating can slow or reduce the absorption of oral medication taken at the same time. This is not a drug-interaction in the usual sense; it is a physical effect on absorption timing.

The practical fix is straightforward: space any coating and soothing herb preparation at least two hours away from any prescription drug. Take your medication first, wait at least two hours, then take the herbal preparation. Or take the herb preparation first and wait two hours before medication. Do not take them together.
The rule

Before starting any herbal preparation, check both the herb and all the medication you are currently taking. The check has two parts: reading the safety notes on the herb's individual page on this site. And then raising it with a pharmacist, a qualified herbalist, or your prescriber.

A community pharmacist is usually the fastest and most accessible first point of contact. Pharmacists are trained in drug interactions and have access to interaction databases. They see the combination of your medication from the dispensing record. A pharmacist conversation takes a few minutes and often resolves the question immediately.
A qualified herbalist can help with herb-specific knowledge. They are most useful for complex prescriptions or for herbs not in standard pharmacist databases.

Your prescriber is the right call when the drug is one of the high-stakes ones listed above: immunosuppressants. HIV medication, anticoagulants, oral contraceptives, cancer drugs, cardiac drugs. These are the cases where a brief conversation before starting could prevent a serious outcome.
For readers on no prescription medication

If you take no prescription medication, the herb-drug interaction risk is much lower. Read each herb's safety notes for allergen flags, pregnancy guidance, and any over-the-counter interactions. The high-stakes interactions are mainly for readers on prescription drugs.
